extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP scholars, law students, and judges interested in claim construction and doctrine of equivalents
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical criteria for assessing patent infringement under the doctrine of equivalents, illustrated by the Epilady litigation and comparing UK and German tests for claim interpretation and equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposive construction (Catnic / Lord Diplock)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification should be given a purposive construction rather than a purely literal one; the question is whether persons with practical knowledge would understand that strict compliance with a particular descriptive word or phrase was intended by the patentee to be an essential requirement of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid meticulous verbal analysis; interpret claims in light of practical knowledge of the relevant art. Use Lord Diplock's Catnic formulation as the baseline for construing specifications under the Patents Act/EPC Protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoffmann's three-question test (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether a variant embodied in an alleged infringing product falls within the claim as properly interpreted, the court should ask: (1) does the variant have a material effect on the way the invention works; (2) would it have been obvious at the publication date to a skilled reader that the variant has no material effect; and (3) would a skilled reader nonetheless have understood from the claim language that the patentee intended strict compliance with the primary meaning?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the three questions sequentially: materiality (fact), obviousness (fact), and patentee intent/construction (construction). A negative at any stage generally leads to no infringement, but the third question is one of construction and can override the first two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question (1): Material effect on the way the invention works
rubrics_metrics.description: If the variant has a material effect upon the way the invention works, the variant is outside the claim and there is no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two key guidelines: (a) a 'variant' is a feature in the alleged infringing product not within the literal or contextual meaning of a claim term; (b) whether the variant makes a material difference is a question of fact (not construction) and must be sensibly answered with reference to the patent. Describe the invention's working at the same level of generality as the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question (2): Obviousness at the date of publication to a skilled reader
rubrics_metrics.description: If it would not have been obvious at the patent publication date to a person skilled in the art that the variant has no material effect, the variant is outside the claim; if it would have been obvious, proceed to question three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question two is a question of fact. The hypothetical skilled person is assumed to be told of both the invention and the variant and asked whether the variant would obviously work in the same way. Expert evidence on what would have been obvious is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question (3): Whether the skilled reader would construe the claim as excluding the variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the reader skilled in the art have nevertheless understood from the language of the claim that the patentee intended strict compliance with the primary (literal) meaning as an essential requirement of the invention? If yes, the variant is outside the claim and there is no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a question of construction (not fact); answers to the first two questions are not conclusive. Consider the claim language, specification (including any 'equivalents clause'), drawings, and expert views about how a skilled reader would understand the patentee's intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of an 'equivalents clause' in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A general statement in the description that embodiments are 'illustrative and not restrictive' and that 'all variations which come within the meaning and range of equivalency of the claims are intended to be embraced' can be evidence regarding patentee intent to include equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may read such a clause as directing that claims be construed purposively under Catnic/Protocol, but the clause does not automatically broaden claims to include variants if a skilled reader would construe the claim literally. How the clause is interpreted depends on context and expert evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/Protocol interpretive rule (Section 125 / Protocol on Article 69 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the Patents Act (and corresponding EPC Article 69), an invention is taken to be that specified in the claim as interpreted by the description and any drawings; the Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are to be interpreted by reference to the specification and drawings, with the Protocol guiding balance between literal scope and scope indicated by description. This statutory framework governs purposive construction analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: German two-question test for equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The German District Court applied a two-question test: (1) does the alleged equivalent have the identical effect as the claimed element (i.e., is it an equivalent); and (2) would the alleged equivalent have been an obvious equivalent to a person skilled in the art from the prospective viewpoint at the time the patent was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court begins by using the claim to determine the patent's 'teaching.' Both questions involve factual inquiry (identical effect) and an obviousness assessment at the patent issue date; if both are satisfied, infringement can be found under equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of expert testimony in equivalence and construction inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert witnesses are used to address factual questions (material effect; obviousness) and to inform how a person skilled in the art would understand claims, specification, and any equivalents clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts may present competing views on whether a variant makes a material difference, whether it would have been obvious to substitute, and whether the specification indicates an intent to cover alternatives. Courts weigh expert evidence in applying factual and construction questions.
